progression.startsWith: Last time, we saw that the rows and columns of the periodic table follow electron shells. Here's a puzzle from that table. Sodium and chlorine sit in the same row. A chlorine atom has six more protons and six more electrons than a sodium atom. So you'd expect it to be bigger. It's not. Chlorine's atom is much smaller. And go down a column, from lithium to potassium, and atoms get larger. So why does atomic radius change across a period and down a group?

teaching.task: # Year 11 Chemistry M1 V13: Atomic radius trends. Why does atomic radius change across a period and down a group? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: An atom has no hard edge, so chemists measure the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together, and take half. That's the atomic radius. It's tiny, so we use picometres. A picometre is a millionth of a millionth of a metre. Every value we compare today is measured the same way, so the comparison is fair. Two things decide how close the outer electrons sit. The first is the nucleus. Its positive protons attract the negative electrons, and more protons pull harder. The second is shielding. Inner electrons sit between the nucleus and the outer electrons, and their repulsion cancels part of the nucleus's pull. A simple way to estimate the pull an outer electron feels is the core charge: the number of protons, minus the number of inner electrons. For sodium, that's eleven minus ten, so plus one. Exam answers call this net pull the effective nuclear charge. Now go across Period three, from sodium to chlorine. Each step adds one proton to the nucleus. The new electron goes into the same third shell, so the inner shells don't change, and there are still ten inner electrons. So the core charge climbs, from plus one for sodium to plus seven for chlorine. A stronger pull on the same shell draws the outer electrons closer, and the atom gets smaller.

# Year 11 Chemistry M1 V13: Atomic radius trends. Why does atomic radius change across a period and down a group? (design)

Status: Revision 3 (7 Nov 2026): brief 186 error check clean (root confirmed); headline count restated as the sum of scene strings. Ready to voice. Previously Revision 2 (6 Nov 2026): brief 178 review repairs applied. Needs a Codex error check before voicing. Summary: radius uses two identical bonded atoms; 11+ kept on the nucleus; "same core charge". Narration 5,613 characters (joined parser count), about 509.4 s. Previously Revision 1 (5 November 2026): first design. Needs independent learning review and science check before voicing.

Narration 5,597 characters (sum of scene strings; 5,613 with joining spaces; Revision 1 was 5,621 by the joined parser count), 17 scenes, about 509.4 s (8.5 minutes), counted by script with the build parser rules (see "Narration length estimate"). Nothing recorded; human listening pending. Voice: the Google voice (all Year 11).

Scope: thirteenth video of Year 11 Chemistry (2017 syllabus), Module 1; first of the periodic-trend videos (v13 radius, v14 ionisation energy and electronegativity, v15 reactivity with water). Templates: `phys-y11-fa1-v01.md` (structure), `chem-y11-m1-v10.md` (series conventions), `bio-y11-fa1-v05.md` (asset brief format). No starter pack exists for this video; the pack work (exact syllabus wording, site read, independent data and arithmetic, original questions, asset check) is done here. Route entry: `chem-y11-m1-v13` in `../../programme/chem-y11-route-inputs.json`. Site lesson read in full (5 November, read-only): `C:/Users/kygs/hscscience/subjects/chemistry/year11/module1/lesson17.sa.html` (SHA256 `f5255f5050cd01fd277fb04e8830faf13d54b88bc8fc9efd1eaeed42a5715665`, recomputed, matches the route; used: the hook, `l17-the-main-atomic-radius-trend-title`, `l17-how-to-explain-the-trend-in-exam-language-title`, `l17-atoms-compared-with-ions-title`, the misconception card, the Na, Mg, Al worked example and drills 1, 4 and 5). Site corrections file checked: no logged item touches lesson 17.

Owner rules applied: as v08 to v10 (one learner question; no people, hands or faces; atoms drawn as coded shell models in the HSC convention, no painted plates needed; 3 s prediction countdown; "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown and the full question on screen; brief feedback with one crossed mistake; original HSC-style questions; optional key notes; Australian spelling; no em dashes; nothing in the bottom 12% of the frame).

Syllabus content (Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 1; local ledger ID `C1-IQ3-01`), quoted from `../../programme/syllabus/chem-2017-y11.json`:

- "demonstrate, explain and predict the relationships in the observable trends in the physical and chemical properties of elements in periods and groups in the periodic table, including but not limited to:"
  - "electronic configurations and atomic radii" (this video)
  - "first ionisation energy and electronegativity" (v14), "reactivity with water" (v15), "state of matter at room temperature" (v12)

Source: https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-03/chemistry-stage6-syllabus-word.docx (page 37)

**Boundary:** opens on v12's final frame (assumed; see Decisions). Teaches what an atomic radius measures (half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together, in picometres); the two competing effects on an outer electron (attraction to the nucleus, shielding by inner electrons) with core charge as a simple counting estimate; why radius decreases across Period 3 (same shells, rising core charge); why adding electrons to the same shell does not make the atom bigger; why radius increases down Group 1 (an extra occupied shell each step, same core charge); exam sentences; atoms against their ions (Na and Na⁺, Cl and Cl⁻) and an isoelectronic set, so electron count is never the only cause. Stops before ionisation energy and electronegativity (v14, the handoff), reactivity (v15) and transition-metal radii (one grey tag).

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "Why does atomic radius change across a period and down a group?" It is already causal. The answer, in order: radius is a measured distance (2); two effects act on outer electrons (3); across a period the shells stay the same while the pull grows (4, 5); down a group each step adds a shell (7); ions change the electrons around the same nucleus (9, 10).
- **Opening frame (reconciled by root, 5 November).** v13 opens on v12's actual final frame: period 3 row and Li to K group 1 column outlined on `PeriodicGrid`, Na, Cl and K shell diagrams in dashed "radius?" circles. Scene 1 fades the circles and keeps K for the down-group beat.
- **Surprise first (site hook).** "Cram more protons and more electrons into an atom and it gets smaller." Chlorine has six more protons and six more electrons than sodium, yet its radius is 102 pm against sodium's 166 pm. The video then explains it.
- **Real data, not invented values (author note a).** Atomic radii are Cordero et al. (2008) covalent radii, the measure the site describes ("roughly half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms"). Ionic radii are Shannon (1976) six-coordinate values. On screen: Period 3 Na 166, Mg 141, Al 121, Si 111, P 107, S 105, Cl 102 pm; Group 1 Li 128, Na 166, K 203, Rb 220, Cs 244 pm; ions Na⁺ 102, Cl⁻ 181, O²⁻ 140, F⁻ 133, Mg²⁺ 72, Al³⁺ 54 pm. A grey Sources tag sits under each bar chart. Argon is left off the period chart (site complication 1: noble-gas radii are measured on a different basis), with a grey tag saying so.
- **Core charge as a counting estimate (author note b).** The site uses effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) qualitatively. Year 11 students need a number they can work out, so the video uses core charge: protons minus inner-shell electrons (sodium 11 − 10 = +1; chlorine 17 − 10 = +7; lithium 3 − 2 = +1; potassium 19 − 18 = +1). It is introduced as "a simple estimate of the pull an outer electron feels" and the term "effective nuclear charge" is named once as the exam phrase for the same idea. Assumptions checked in "Memory aid check".
- **Shielding in plain words.** "Inner electrons sit between the nucleus and the outer electrons, and their repulsion cancels part of the nucleus's pull." Electrons in the same shell shield each other only a little (site misconception card), which is the cause scene 5 uses.
- **Down a group (site).** Each step down Group 1 adds an occupied shell; core charge stays +1; the outer electron is further out and the extra shell outweighs the extra protons. The site's "more shielded" is kept but the main cause spoken is distance (extra shell), matching the site's fast rule ("extra occupied shells win").
- **Ions without "electron count only" (route stop).** Na → Na⁺: the whole third shell is lost (2,8,1 → 2,8), so the outer electrons are now in the second shell (site trap: "not one tiny dot"). Cl → Cl⁻: one extra electron in the same shell, same 17 protons, more repulsion, the cloud spreads. Isoelectronic set (site drill 5): five species with 10 electrons each shrink as proton number rises, so the same electron count gives different sizes. The ionic and atomic radii come from different measurements, so comparisons are of direction and rough size only (author note c).
- **In-teaching prediction (3 s, scenes 6 and 7).** Lithium or potassium: which atom is larger? (Site quick check 1.)
- **Memory aid:** "Across: same shells, stronger pull. Down: one more shell each step." (Site's fast rule, reworded so each half names its cause.) Checked in "Memory aid check".
- **Attempts (original wording, HSC style).** A1: magnesium 141 pm and sulfur 105 pm; explain why sulfur atoms are smaller even though they have more electrons. Crossed: "sulfur has fewer shells". A2: oxygen atom 66 pm; predict and explain the size of O²⁻. Answer: larger (140 pm). Crossed: "O²⁻ has an extra shell".
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. "More electrons make a bigger atom" (5, from the site's misconception card); "Na⁺ is Na minus one tiny dot" (9); "electron count alone sets ion size" (10); "sulfur has fewer shells" (crossed in 13); "an anion gains a shell" (crossed in 15).
- **Handoff (route next: `chem-y11-m1-v14`, "How do first ionisation energy and electronegativity follow atomic structure?").** Scene 16 turns the result into a question: a smaller atom with a stronger pull should hold its electrons more tightly. Final frame: the sodium and chlorine shell models from scene 4, an energy arrow pulling sodium's outer electron away with "energy?", a second chlorine pulling on a shared pair with "pull?", and the chip "Next: how do first ionisation energy and electronegativity follow atomic structure?".
- **Site notes (read 5 November; for root to log in `../site-corrections-chem-y11.md` if accepted):**
  1. `l17-the-main-atomic-radius-trend-title`, down-group row: "Outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the atom is larger." Acceptable, but core charge is unchanged down a group, so "more shielded" alone does not explain the size; the extra occupied shell does. Suggest leading with the extra shell (as the site's own fast rule does). Minor.
  2. `l17-atoms-compared-with-ions-title`, isoelectronic list "Al³⁺ < Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < O²⁻": correct (Shannon 54, 72, 102, 133, 140 pm). Noted as checked.
  3. No numerical radii are given on the site; the values used here are sourced (author note a).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) a radius is half the distance between bonded nuclei (2); (2) outer electrons feel the nucleus's pull, reduced by inner-electron shielding; core charge estimates the net pull (3); (3) across a period the shells stay the same while core charge rises, so outer electrons are pulled closer (4); (4) added electrons go into the same shell and shield each other little, so more electrons do not mean a bigger atom (5); (5) down a group each step adds a shell, core charge stays the same, so the outer electron is further out (7); (6) losing a whole shell shrinks a cation; extra repulsion in the same shell grows an anion (9); (7) with the same electron count, more protons pull harder (10).
- **Entry knowledge:** Stage 5 atoms with electron shells; v08 (protons, electrons, Z), v11 (configurations), v12 (period = number of occupied shells; group = valence electrons for Groups 1 and 2, valence electrons = group number minus 10 for Groups 13 to 17; metals and non-metals).
- **Learner-visible vocabulary:** atomic radius (half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the element, 2); picometre (a millionth of a millionth of a metre, 2); shielding (inner electrons cancelling part of the nucleus's pull on outer electrons, 3); core charge (protons minus inner electrons, a simple estimate of that net pull, 3); effective nuclear charge (the exam term for the net pull, 3); cation and anion (positive and negative ion, 9); isoelectronic (having the same number of electrons, 10).
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Explainer motion (coded):** **shell atom** (nucleus with a proton count, concentric shell rings, electron dots; the outer ring's radius animates to the scaled radius, and a radius ruler from nucleus to outer ring reads the pm value); **pull and shield arrows** (amber arrows from nucleus to outer electrons, thinned by a grey shield band at the inner shells; core charge written in the nucleus as "+1", "+7"); **radius bars** (bars in pm with the Sources tag; one bar grows per element as named); **cross on the table** (the highlighted row and column from v12's frame, with direction arrows "smaller" and "larger"); **ion morph** (an atom's shells morph into its ion: a shell fades out for Na⁺, a dot joins and the ring widens for Cl⁻); `Countdown`, `QuestionCard`, `Chip` with `cross`, `PenArrow`, scribble circle, `HandText`, `KeyNotes`, `Heading`.
- **Board layout (constant):** heading top left; atom models at the left two thirds; radius bars at the right third; the small periodic cross top right as a locator.

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) Covalent radii from B. Cordero et al., "Covalent radii revisited", Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832 to 2838 (doi 10.1039/b801115j), read from the Wikipedia "Covalent radius" table on 5 November 2026: Li 128, Na 166, K 203, Rb 220, Cs 244; Mg 141, Al 121, Si 111, P 107, S 105, Cl 102, Ar 106 (not shown); O 66, F 57. Ionic radii: R. D. Shannon, Acta Cryst. A32 (1976) 751 (six-coordinate effective radii, read from the Wikipedia "Ionic radius" table): Na⁺ 102, Cl⁻ 181, O²⁻ 140, F⁻ 133, Mg²⁺ 72, Al³⁺ 53.5 (shown as 54). Other radius sets (single-bond Pyykkö radii, metallic radii) give different numbers but the same main-group trends here; quote "covalent radius" on the Sources tag.
(b) Core charge = Z − inner-shell electrons. It assumes inner electrons shield completely and same-shell electrons not at all. Slater's rules give Z_eff ≈ 2.2 (Na) and 6.1 (Cl), the same direction. Core charge does not explain transition-metal radii or the small irregularities; not used for those.
(c) Ionic radii (from ionic crystals) and covalent radii (from molecules and covalent solids) are measured on different bases. "Na⁺ is much smaller than Na" and "Cl⁻ is much larger than Cl" are robust; the exact ratios are not taught.
(d) Transition metals: radii change little across the d-block (site complication 2); grey tag in scene 4 only.
(e) Pronunciations: "picometre" (PIE-co-mee-ter); "isoelectronic"; "Al three plus" spoken as "aluminium three plus".

Main question: *Why does atomic radius change across a period and down a group?*
Entry knowledge: Stage 5 shells; v08, v11, v12.
Stops after: radius defined, shielding and core charge, the period and group trends with sourced data, exam sentences, atoms against ions and an isoelectronic set. No ionisation energy, electronegativity, reactivity or transition-metal explanation.
Handoff: chem-y11-m1-v14, first ionisation energy and electronegativity.

## Script and shots

Cue words in **bold** trigger the visual change. Colour key (continues v08 to v10): protons and the nucleus red (`C.rose`); electrons blue (`C.blue`); shell rings ink; core charge and pull arrows amber; shielding band grey; radius ruler teal; crossed chips red strike.

- **Explainer motion (coded):** **shell atom** (nucleus with a proton count, concentric shell rings, electron dots; the outer ring's radius animates to the scaled radius, and a radius ruler from nucleus to outer ring reads the pm value); **pull and shield arrows** (amber arrows from nucleus to outer electrons, thinned by a grey shield band at the inner shells; core charge written in the nucleus as "+1", "+7"); **radius bars** (bars in pm with the Sources tag; one bar grows per element as named); **cross on the table** (the highlighted row and column from v12's frame, with direction arrows "smaller" and "larger"); **ion morph** (an atom's shells morph into its ion: a shell fades out for Na⁺, a dot joins and the ring widens for Cl⁻); `Countdown`, `QuestionCard`, `Chip` with `cross`, `PenArrow`, scribble circle, `HandText`, `KeyNotes`, `Heading`.
- **Board layout (constant):** heading top left; atom models at the left two thirds; radius bars at the right third; the small periodic cross top right as a locator.

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) Covalent radii from B. Cordero et al., "Covalent radii revisited", Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832 to 2838 (doi 10.1039/b801115j), read from the Wikipedia "Covalent radius" table on 5 November 2026: Li 128, Na 166, K 203, Rb 220, Cs 244; Mg 141, Al 121, Si 111, P 107, S 105, Cl 102, Ar 106 (not shown); O 66, F 57. Ionic radii: R. D. Shannon, Acta Cryst. A32 (1976) 751 (six-coordinate effective radii, read from the Wikipedia "Ionic radius" table): Na⁺ 102, Cl⁻ 181, O²⁻ 140, F⁻ 133, Mg²⁺ 72, Al³⁺ 53.5 (shown as 54). Other radius sets (single-bond Pyykkö radii, metallic radii) give different numbers but the same main-group trends here; quote "covalent radius" on the Sources tag.
(b) Core charge = Z − inner-shell electrons. It assumes inner electrons shield completely and same-shell electrons not at all. Slater's rules give Z_eff ≈ 2.2 (Na) and 6.1 (Cl), the same direction. Core charge does not explain transition-metal radii or the small irregularities; not used for those.
(c) Ionic radii (from ionic crystals) and covalent radii (from molecules and covalent solids) are measured on different bases. "Na⁺ is much smaller than Na" and "Cl⁻ is much larger than Cl" are robust; the exact ratios are not taught.
(d) Transition metals: radii change little across the d-block (site complication 2); grey tag in scene 4 only.
(e) Pronunciations: "picometre" (PIE-co-mee-ter); "isoelectronic"; "Al three plus" spoken as "aluminium three plus".

Main question: *Why does atomic radius change across a period and down a group?*
Entry knowledge: Stage 5 shells; v08, v11, v12.
Stops after: radius defined, shielding and core charge, the period and group trends with sourced data, exam sentences, atoms against ions and an isoelectronic set. No ionisation energy, electronegativity, reactivity or transition-metal explanation.
Handoff: chem-y11-m1-v14, first ionisation energy and electronegativity.

scenes.teachingReason: Two things decide how close the outer electrons sit. The first is the nucleus. Its positive protons attract the negative electrons, and more protons pull harder. The second is shielding. Inner electrons sit between the nucleus and the outer electrons, and their repulsion cancels part of the nucleus's pull. A simple way to estimate the pull an outer electron feels is the core charge: the number of protons, minus the number of inner electrons. For sodium, that's eleven minus ten, so plus one. Exam answers call this net pull the effective nuclear charge.

scenes.teachingReason: Atoms can also gain or lose electrons to form ions. When sodium loses its one outer electron, it doesn't just lose a dot. It loses the whole third shell. The extra electron adds repulsion between the outer electrons, so they spread out, and the chloride ion is larger.

scenes.motionPurpose:
### 17. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".
> Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

1. Atomic radius: half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms of an element (in pm; 1 pm = 10⁻¹² m).
2. Across a period, radius decreases: protons increase, electrons enter the same shell, shielding barely changes, so the effective nuclear charge (core charge = protons − inner electrons) rises and pulls the outer electrons closer.
3. Down a group, radius increases: each element has an extra occupied shell, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus (core charge stays the same).
4. Cations are smaller than their atoms (often a whole shell is lost); anions are larger (same protons, more electron repulsion). For isoelectronic ions, more protons means a smaller ion.

### 17. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".
> Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

1. Atomic radius: half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms of an element (in pm; 1 pm = 10⁻¹² m).
2. Across a period, radius decreases: protons increase, electrons enter the same shell, shielding barely changes, so the effective nuclear charge (core charge = protons − inner electrons) rises and pulls the outer electrons closer.
3. Down a group, radius increases: each element has an extra occupied shell, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus (core charge stays the same).
4. Cations are smaller than their atoms (often a whole shell is lost); anions are larger (same protons, more electron repulsion). For isoelectronic ions, more protons means a smaller ion.
